newsitem.title: USA: After Denver, Clinton turns to domestic concerns.
newsitem.headline: After Denver, Clinton turns to domestic concerns.

text.p: Shifting gears from the international diplomacy of the Denver summit, President Clinton Monday turned to the domestic scene and unveiled three steps to encourage home ownership in U.S. inner cities.

During a 24-hour visit to California, Clinton also planned to attend three fund-raisers to benefit the Democratic Party, which is deeply in debt following his re-election victory, and Sen. Barbara Boxer, a California Democrat.
Speaking to the U.S. Conference of Mayors, Clinton argued that American cities are in better shape because of the economic recovery but said they have not enjoyed its full benefits.
"We have got to keep working until we extend the prosperity of this recovery to every neighbourhood in America," Clinton told the mayors.

The White House timed Clinton's speech to co-incide with the release of a federal report that found cities facing three key problems: urban unemployment remains higher than suburban and national rates; the poor have become more concentrated in inner cities, and middle class city flight continues.
Clinton announced three steps to help people buy homes in inner cities:

-- The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) will begin a one-year programme to make it cheaper for police officers to buy homes in the neighbourhoods where they work by allowing them to buy HUD-foreclosed properties for half price. HUD hopes 1,000 police officers will take up the offer.

-- The Federal Housing Administration will cut its mortgage insurance premiums by 25 basis points to 1.5 percent for first time homebuyers in the largest U.S. cities, saving them $200 on an average $85,000 mortgage.

-- The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. will begin a test programme to help up to 2,000 low-income people buy homes by allowing them to use their Section 8 federal rent subsidies for mortgage payments.
HUD Secretary Andrew Cuomo told reporters that the three programmes would cost the government $700 million annually and said the funds would come from HUD's budget.

The small-scale measures were characteristic of Clinton's second-term proposals, where he has looked for initiatives that require little new federal money at a time when the government is seeking to eliminate the federal budget deficit by 2002.

In another such initiative, Clinton was to announce later in the day in Los Angeles that a private company, Kaiser Permanente, would spend $100 million to provide health care coverage to up to 50,000 uninsured children in California.
After speaking to the mayors, Clinton was to attend one fund-raiser each in San Francisco and Los Angeles to benefit Boxer, who is expected to face a tough and expensive re-election fight in 1998.
At the end of the day, Clinton was to attend a late-night fund-raiser in Los Angeles to raise about $80,000 for the Democratic Party before returning to Washington early Tuesday.
